470.title: Ashtpadi 9, salok: the true names
470.hook: the salok turns to what the true devotee is like
470.howItsDone: Sikhism has no priestly caste: any Sikh may read the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs read ashtpadi nine of Sukhmani Sahib as a call to live up to a name rather than rest on it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, living ashtpadi eight: a child in her father's shoes, and a portrait to grow into. Your line was grow into it. Which quality did you try on? Today, ashtpadi nine. Day four hundred seventy.

Every age has its religious job titles. Reverend. Doctor of divinity. Elder. In Guru Arjan's Punjab, around 1600, there were plenty too, and people heard them every day: pandit, the learned one; vaishnav, the devotee of Vishnu; and aparas, the untouched one, a holy man who kept himself ritually apart, never touching anything that might make him impure. Ashtpadi nine takes these honored names one by one. It doesn't mock them. It does something more interesting. It asks what each name would look like if it were true all the way through.
screen: `EVERY AGE HAS ITS TITLES.` → `PANDIT, VAISHNAV, APARAS.` → `WHAT IF EACH WERE TRUE?`

segments.voice: The salok begins with the last of those names. Whoever keeps the Name enshrined in the heart, and sees God in everyone, and bows to the Master moment by moment: Nanak, that one is the true aparas, and saves all. Notice the swap. The aparas of the day kept apart from other people to stay pure. Guru Arjan's aparas sees God in everyone, which is the opposite of keeping apart. The purity is still there, but it's moved. It's not about what your hands avoid. It's about what your heart holds. The first stanza fills it in: the true aparas is one whose tongue never touches a lie, whose eyes don't look with lust at another's spouse, who loves the company of the holy. The untouched one is untouched by falsehood. That's the pattern of the whole ashtpadi. Each stanza takes a respected title and pours new content into it, a life to match the name. And it says nothing against the people who held those titles sincerely. It just won't let the name do the work by itself. This fits the Sikh path closely. Sikhism has no priestly caste. A granthi who reads in the gurdwara is a respected servant of the community, not a holy class apart, and any Sikh, woman or man, may read the Guru Granth Sahib. So the question ashtpadi nine keeps asking is not what are you called, but what are you like.
screen: `APARAS: THE UNTOUCHED ONE.` · `NOT APART: SEEING GOD IN ALL.` · `UNTOUCHED BY FALSEHOOD.` · `A LIFE TO MATCH THE NAME.` · then, large: `TRUE, NOT TITLED.`

segments.voice: The practice: think what makes a person true. Picture someone with an impressive title, a doctor, a judge, a teacher, a religious leader. Now picture someone with no title at all who is completely trustworthy. Which one would you call at two in the morning? Let that answer settle. Then turn the question round, gently, toward yourself. Not what you're called. What you're like, when no one's watching. Breathe in: the name. Breathe out: the life. The bell holds the time.
Ashtpadi nine. Its salok names the true aparas: not the one who keeps apart, but the one who sees God in all.
Your line: true, not titled. Today, when someone's title impresses you, ask quietly what their life is like, and then ask it of your own. Day four hundred seventy.

471.title: The true scholar
471.hook: the true pandit is one who instructs his own mind
471.howItsDone: Sikhs value study of Gurbani through katha and personal reading, and read this stanza of Sukhmani Sahib as a reminder that learning should first change the learner.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the salok of ashtpadi 9: the true aparas, untouched by falsehood, seeing God in all. Your line was true, not titled. Today, ashtpadi nine takes up another title: the scholar. Day four hundred seventy-one.

Everyone knows someone who can win any argument and still can't stop checking their phone at dinner. Or a brilliant expert who gives wonderful advice and never takes any of it. Knowing a lot and being changed by what you know are two very different things. Students cram for an exam and forget it all a week later. Teachers explain patience beautifully and lose their temper at the photocopier. In the Guru's day, the pandit was the learned one, the scholar who knew the old texts and taught them. Ashtpadi nine asks: who does the true pandit teach first?
screen: `WINS EVERY ARGUMENT.` → `NEVER TAKES HIS OWN ADVICE.` → `WHO DOES THE PANDIT TEACH FIRST?`

segments.voice: The stanza opens: so pandit jo man parbodhai. That one is a pandit who instructs his own mind. Parbodh means to awaken, to teach, to bring to understanding. The first student is the self. The next line: he searches for the Lord's Name within his own soul. Then: he drinks the sweet essence of the Name, and by that pandit's teaching the world lives. Then a line that tells you this pandit is not rejecting learning: he understands the root of the old scriptures, and sees the large hidden in the small. So the true scholar still reads. But the reading has gone somewhere. It's gone inward first, and come back out as a life. And then a line with real weight in sixteenth-century India: he gives teaching to all four castes. In a world where sacred learning was often kept within one group, the stanza's ideal scholar teaches everyone. Sikh tradition takes that seriously: the Guru Granth Sahib is read aloud in Punjabi script, in the common languages of the people, to anyone who walks into the gurdwara. The stanza ends with Nanak bowing, forever, to that kind of pandit. So the order matters. Teach your own mind first. Then, and only then, your teaching might keep the world alive. Notice this isn't anti-intellectual. Sikh history is full of scholars, poets and copyists. It's about which direction the learning flows.
screen: `SO PANDIT: HE TEACHES HIS OWN MIND.` · `SEARCHING THE NAME WITHIN.` · `HE TEACHES ALL FOUR CASTES.` · `INWARD FIRST, THEN OUT AS A LIFE.` · then, large: `TEACH YOUR OWN MIND.`

segments.voice: The practice: teach yourself one thing. Pick a piece of advice you often give other people. Slow down. Drink water. Don't take it personally. Say it now, silently, to yourself, as if you were the student and also the teacher. Then ask your mind, kindly: did you hear that? Sit with the answer, whatever it is, without scolding. Breathe in: the teacher speaks. Breathe out: the student listens. If you pray, you can ask for an awakened mind. The bell holds the time.
The true scholar. So pandit jo man parbodhai: the real pandit is the one who instructs his own mind, and then teaches everyone.
Your line: teach your own mind. Today, before you give anyone advice, try it on yourself first, once. Day four hundred seventy-one.

472.title: The true devotee
472.hook: titles mean nothing without the life that matches
472.howItsDone: Sikhs practice seva, selfless service, in the gurdwara and beyond, and read these stanzas of Sukhmani Sahib as describing devotion that seeks no reward.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the true scholar: the pandit who teaches his own mind first. Your line was teach your own mind. Did you try your own advice? Today, ashtpadi nine turns to the devotee. Day four hundred seventy-two.

Someone volunteers at a shelter every Saturday, and makes sure to post a photo every time. Someone else drives an elderly neighbor to the doctor every month for years and never mentions it to anyone. Both did good. But if you had to guess which one was really devoted, you'd probably guess the second. Not because photos are wicked. Because the second one clearly wasn't waiting for anything back. Ashtpadi nine has two stanzas about devotees, and both of them land on exactly that point.
screen: `A PHOTO EVERY SATURDAY.` → `A NEIGHBOR DRIVEN FOR YEARS.` → `WHO WASN'T WAITING FOR ANYTHING?`

segments.voice: One stanza takes the title vaishnav, a devotee of Vishnu, a name honored across India. It says: the true vaishnav is the one with whom God is well pleased, who lives apart from the pull of maya, the passing world. Then the striking line: karam karat hovai nihkaram. Doing deeds, he remains without deeds. Nihkaram means free of the deed, free of its grip. It doesn't mean doing nothing. It means doing the good thing without hooking yourself to the result. The stanza says it plainly in the next lines: he doesn't hanker after the fruit of any action; he is absorbed only in devotion and the singing of praise. The next stanza takes another devotee's title, bhagauti, and says the same in a different key: the true one is dyed in love for God, leaves bad company behind, and every doubt dissolves from the mind. Two titles, one point. Devotion is measured by the life underneath it, and especially by whether it's waiting for a reward. The neighbor who drives someone to the doctor for years isn't keeping score. That's karam karat hovai nihkaram. The deed is done. The doer isn't clinging. This is not a criticism of the people who held these titles; the stanzas honor the names by asking them to be true. It's a mirror, held up to anyone who calls themselves devoted, in any community. Sikhs have a word for selfless service: seva. Its whole point is the same: the life, not the title.
screen: `VAISHNAV: AN HONORED NAME.` · `NIHKARAM: DOING, BUT NOT GRIPPED.` · `NO HANKERING FOR THE FRUIT.` · `BHAGAUTI: DYED IN LOVE.` · then, large: `THE LIFE, NOT THE TITLE.`

segments.voice: The practice: live one value quietly. Choose one value you care about: kindness, honesty, patience, generosity. Now picture one small act of it you could do today, where no one will see, and you won't mention it afterward. Wiping a shared table. Paying a compliment to someone's back. Leaving a good review for a stranger's small shop. Hold that picture. Notice any little wish to be noticed, and let it go on the out-breath. Breathe in: the deed. Breathe out: no reward. The bell holds the time.
The true devotee. Karam karat hovai nihkaram: doing deeds, yet free of them, hankering after no reward.
Your line: the life, not the title. Today, do your quiet good deed, and don't tell anyone, not even tonight. Day four hundred seventy-two.

473.title: Living ashtpadi 9
473.hook: drop one title and keep the substance
473.howItsDone: Many Sikhs use the names Singh and Kaur, given at the founding of the Khalsa, in place of or alongside caste surnames, and read ashtpadi nine of Sukhmani Sahib as a call to substance over status.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the true devotee: doing deeds, free of them, seeking no reward. Your line was the life, not the title. Did your quiet deed stay quiet? Today, we live ashtpadi nine. Day four hundred seventy-three.

Meet a Sikh family and you'll often notice something about the names. The father is a Singh. The son is a Singh. The mother is a Kaur, and so is the daughter, and so is the grandmother, and so, quite possibly, is the woman from a completely different village who runs the gurdwara kitchen. In much of South Asia a surname can tell a stranger your caste, your clan, your rank. Many Sikh names deliberately tell them nothing of the kind. That's ashtpadi nine, carried into everyday life.
screen: `A FAMILY OF SINGHS AND KAURS.` → `SURNAMES THAT TELL YOUR RANK.` → `NAMES THAT DELIBERATELY DON'T.`

segments.voice: Ashtpadi nine took the honored titles of its day, the aparas, the vaishnav, the bhagauti, the pandit, and poured a matching life into each one. Untouched by falsehood. Doing good, not gripped by reward. Teaching your own mind first. Its message, stanza after stanza: the name is nothing without the substance underneath it. Nearly a century later, Sikh tradition remembers Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Guru, making that idea visible. When he founded the Khalsa in 1699, tradition says he gave the initiated men the name Singh, meaning lion, and the women the name Kaur, often explained as princess. The same names for everyone, whatever family or caste they came from. Many Sikhs today use Singh or Kaur in place of a caste surname, and many use both alongside a family name; there's real variety. But the idea behind the custom is the one Guru Arjan was teaching in Sukhmani. Titles that rank people don't decide who someone is. Living ashtpadi nine, for any of us, can be smaller than a new name. It can be letting go of one title in your own head: the clever one, the responsible one, the one who's always right, the expert. Not the work behind it, just the label. Keep the substance. Drop the badge. Then see if people still know who you are by how you live. Often, they know you better.
screen: `FOUR TITLES, EACH GIVEN A LIFE.` · `1699: SINGH AND KAUR.` · `THE SAME NAMES FOR EVERYONE.` · `DROP THE BADGE, KEEP THE WORK.` · then, large: `SUBSTANCE OVER TITLE.`

segments.voice: The practice: do good without a label. First, name to yourself one title you quietly carry: the smart one, the fixer, the good one, the busy one. Hold it for a moment. Then imagine setting it down beside you, like a heavy bag. Breathe. Who are you without it? Probably the same person, just lighter. Today, do one good thing without that label attached: help without being the helper, know something without being the expert. If you pray, you can offer the deed without your name on it. The bell holds the time.
Living ashtpadi nine. Drop one title, keep the substance: the name is nothing without the life underneath it.
Your line: substance over title. Today, do one good thing without your usual label on it, and notice who you are without the badge. Day four hundred seventy-three.

474.title: Ashtpadi 10, salok: countless
474.hook: the salok marvels at countless beings
474.howItsDone: Sikhs reading Sukhmani Sahib meet this salok at the opening of the tenth ashtpadi, whose stanzas go on to list the countless beings of the creation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, living ashtpadi nine: Singh and Kaur, and a badge set down. Your line was substance over title. Today, ashtpadi ten, and the camera pulls back. Day four hundred seventy-four.

Stand at a busy train station at rush hour and just watch. Thousands of people, every one of them the main character of their own story. One is late for a job interview. One just got engaged. One is going to visit a mother in hospital. One is humming. You'll never know any of them, and every one of them has a whole inner life as large as yours. It can make you feel very small, or strangely tender. For several ashtpadis, Sukhmani has zoomed in on one kind of person. Now it pulls back, and looks at the crowd.
screen: `A STATION AT RUSH HOUR.` → `EACH ONE A WHOLE STORY.` → `SUKHMANI PULLS BACK.`

segments.voice: The salok of ashtpadi ten has two lines. The first: ustat karahi anek jan. Countless people sing His praise. Ustat is praise; anek is many, more than one can number. And there's no end, no far shore, to it. Ant na paaraavaar: no end, no near bank or far bank. The second line: Nanak, God made the creation in so many ways, of countless kinds. Rachnaa is creation, the thing made, the way a poem or a building is made. Bahu bidh, many ways. Anik prakaar, countless kinds. Notice what's being praised here. Not one perfect person. Not the brahm giaanee of two ashtpadis ago. The sheer number and variety of what exists. In the stanzas that follow, Guru Arjan will list them: people who worship and people who wander, scholars and the lost, worlds beyond worlds. The salok sets the tone for all of it, and the tone is wonder. So many. That's the whole carry, two words, and it's enough. Because when you really take in so many, something shifts. Your own problems are still real, but they're one story among millions. The people who annoy you are also among the so many, each with a whole inner life. And the One who made the creation in all those ways, the salok says, is beyond any shore you could reach. This is the opposite of a crowd making you feel lost. It's a crowd making you feel part of something.
screen: `USTAT: COUNTLESS PEOPLE PRAISE.` · `NO END, NO FAR SHORE.` · `RACHNAA: A CREATION OF MANY KINDS.` · `ONE STORY AMONG MILLIONS.` · then, large: `SO MANY.`

segments.voice: The practice: look at a crowd kindly. If you can, look out a window at people passing, or at faces in a photo, or, eyes closed, picture a busy street you know. Pick out one stranger. Imagine, just for a breath, that they too woke up this morning with worries and hopes. Then another. Then another. Let your face soften as you look. You don't need to know their names. If you pray, you can wish them well in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Ashtpadi ten. Its salok marvels at countless people praising, and a creation made in so many ways.
Your line: so many. Next time you're in a line or a crowd today, look up, and let the two words go through your mind. Day four hundred seventy-four.

475.title: Many millions
475.hook: kaee kott: many millions worship, many millions wander, many millions are learned
475.howItsDone: Sikhs reading Sukhmani Sahib recite the 'kaee kot' stanzas of the tenth ashtpadi in a strong, repeated rhythm, as a hymn of wonder at the size of the creation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tenth salok: countless people praising, a creation of countless kinds. Your line was so many. Did you look up in a crowd? Today the stanzas start counting. Day four hundred seventy-five.

In India, big numbers have their own names. A lakh is a hundred thousand. A crore is ten million. Headlines say a film earned a hundred crore; a festival drew two crore pilgrims. In Punjabi and in the old language of the Guru Granth Sahib, the word is kot, or kott. And ashtpadi ten picks up that enormous number and swings it like a drumstick. Kaee kot. Many crores. Many tens of millions. Line after line after line, in a rhythm you can feel even if you don't understand a single word.
screen: `A LAKH, A CRORE.` → `KOT: TEN MILLION.` → `KAEE KOT, LINE AFTER LINE.`

segments.voice: The first stanza runs like this. Kaee kot hoe poojaaree: many millions are worshippers. Many millions keep religious rites and customs. Many millions live at places of pilgrimage. Many millions wander the forests as renunciates. Many millions listen to the Vedas. Many millions become great ascetics. Many millions fix their minds in meditation. Many millions are poets, pondering poetry. Many millions meditate on the ever-new Name. And then the last line: Nanak, none of them can find the Creator's limit. Notice who's in the list. Worshippers, pilgrims, forest-dwellers, listeners to scripture, ascetics, meditators, poets. Every kind of seeker of Guru Arjan's world, and not one of them is mocked or ranked. They're simply counted, with wonder, as part of the creation. Then comes the turn. All those millions, every path of seeking, and none of them reaches the end of the One who made them. That's not a put-down of the seekers. It's a statement about how big the Creator is. If tens of millions of sincere seekers in every style can't measure it, nobody is going to measure it alone. Sikh teaching says this often, and Japji, which we read last year, says it too: no one can reach the end of God's praise. Kaee kot is that same humility, set to a drumbeat. Millions upon millions, every one of them held. Millions, all His.
screen: `KAEE KOT: MANY TENS OF MILLIONS.` · `WORSHIPPERS, PILGRIMS, POETS.` · `COUNTED, NOT RANKED.` · `NONE FINDS THE CREATOR'S LIMIT.` · then, large: `MILLIONS, ALL HIS.`

segments.voice: The practice: wish well to many millions. Start small. Picture one person who prays differently from you, or doesn't pray at all. Wish them well: may they be safe, may they be at peace. Then picture a town full of people. Wish them well. Then a country. Then the whole planet, eight billion, more than eight hundred crore. You can't picture every face; that's the point. Just let the wish get wider with each breath. If you pray, you can hold them all before God. The bell holds the time.
Many millions. Kaee kot: tens of millions of seekers of every kind, counted with wonder, and none finding the Creator's limit.
Your line: millions, all his. Today, when someone's way of life puzzles you, say the line once in your head before anything else. Day four hundred seventy-five.

476.title: All in His creation
476.hook: the good and the lost are all within His play
476.howItsDone: Sikhs read this stanza of Sukhmani Sahib as a reminder that only the Creator knows the creation, while still standing against injustice as the Gurus taught.

segments.voice: Yesterday, many millions: worshippers, pilgrims, poets, counted with wonder. Your line: millions, all His. Today the count keeps going, into harder territory. Day four hundred seventy-six, the end of a week.

Yesterday's list was easy to love. Pilgrims. Poets. Meditators. If the stanza had stopped there, it would be a nice hymn about good people. It doesn't stop there. The second stanza keeps the same drumbeat, kaee kot, many millions, and turns it on everyone we'd rather leave out of the picture. The proud. The cruel. The thieves. The gossips. The ones chasing money until they drop. It's the kind of list you'd expect before a sermon about who's going to be punished. And that sermon never comes.
screen: `YESTERDAY'S LIST WAS EASY.` → `NOW THE PROUD, THE CRUEL.` → `THE SERMON NEVER COMES.`

segments.voice: The second stanza goes: many millions are proud. Many millions are blind and ignorant. Many millions are misers, hard of heart. Many millions are cold inside, without feeling. Many millions steal what belongs to others. Many millions slander others. Many millions toil for wealth. Many millions wander in foreign lands. Then the turn, addressed straight to God: whatever You attach them to, to that they are attached. And the last line: Nanak, only the Creator knows His own creation. That's it. No verdict. Nobody's sentenced. The stanza simply says: these too are in the creation, and the One who made it is the only one who truly knows it. That doesn't mean Sikh teaching shrugs at cruelty or theft. The Gurus spoke hard words against oppression and greed, and Sikhs are asked to stand up for those who are wronged. But this stanza is about something else: the urge to stand outside the creation and sort it into the saved and the lost, as if we were the one who made it. Kartaa is the word for the Creator, the Doer. Only the Kartaa knows the creation. All of it is within His play. That's humbling, and it's also oddly freeing. You don't have to be everybody's judge today. And this is where the week ends. Seven days ago, the true aparas. Then the true scholar, the true devotee, Singh and Kaur and the badge set down. Then the crowd: so many, many millions, and today, all of them, in the play.

segments.voice: The practice: judge no one today. Begin now. Bring to mind someone you've been judging lately. A relative, a politician, a coworker, a stranger online. Don't argue with your judgment or pretend they're right. Just picture them inside the same creation as you, held by the same hands. Breathe in: they're in the play. Breathe out: so am I. You can still disagree. You can still say no. You're just setting down the gavel for one day. The bell holds the time.
All in His creation. The proud and the lost, the cruel and the kind, many millions, all within His play; only the Creator knows it.
Your line: all in the play. Today, when you feel the gavel coming down on someone, set it down for one breath. Day four hundred seventy-six. A week, done.
